articles.title: Healthcare workers respond to a broken system by unionizing
articles.author: Dennis Kosuth
articles.content_excerpt: C hicago is seeing a burst of unionization amongst registered nurses – and it has become infectious, in the best sense of that word. In May of 2026, 77 percent of nurses at Rush University Medical Center (RUMC) voted in favor of joining the National Nurses Organizing Committee (NNOC). The 1,700 nurses at RUMC are now part of National Nurses United (NNU), a union that represents 225,000 nurses in healthcare settings across the United States. NNU was founded by a merger of nursing unions in 2009 and, in the past 17 years,has grown considerably from its initial strength of 150,000. The latest victory for NNOC took place in the first week of November when nurses who work for Endeavor Health at Edward Hospital in suburban Naperville, voted by a margin of 65 percent in favor of joining the union

The company whose weapons have helped sustain Israel’s genocide in Palestine, its decades-long occupation, and its military assaults on Iran was welcomed as a symbol of industrial progress. articles.title: The end of an era? ANC suffers historic collapse in South Africa
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content_excerpt: South Africa’s Communist Party just broke away at the ballot box: For the first time since the end of apartheid, the SACP ran on its own ticket in municipal elections, winning 271 seats as Nelson Mandela’s ruling ANC party lost its majority on more than 100 councils – its worst-ever election result. Phel Parkies, the SACP’s national head of elections, joins BT Live to break down the historic shift in South African politics. Parkies says the ANC’s showing reflects the party’s “irreversible decline,” having forfeited the peoples’ trust and confidence through collapsing municipal services and the “voracious accumulation” of corrupt local officials. articles.title: The return of the bases: why Filipinos are fighting Pax Silica
articles.author: Atul Chandra
articles.content_excerpt: On Sunday, as Southeast Asian leaders gathered in Manila for the 49th ASEAN Summit, the Philippine police carried out what activists call the largest single-day crackdown in decades of Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s presidency. At Sucat People’s Park in Muntinlupa, a designated freedom park, police took more than 300 people into custody. Eight more were seized at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila as they tried to march towards the summit venue. Television footage showed police brutally arresting and detaining them. articles.title: ‘The city knew’: Who’s to blame for the deadly Brooklyn collapse?
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content_excerpt: “The city knew.” The Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people, including two children, wasn’t a freak accident, says Jaylen Strong, a New York City organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation. It was the predictable result of a housing system where landlords profit from neglect, and where Black, Brown and immigrant tenants pay the price. Joining BT Live’s Zoe Alexandra, Strong points out that a building with nearly 100 open city violations would never have been left to crumble in a wealthier neighborhood. He links the collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue to Trump’s ICE raids that keep families hiding at home, and to a government that has money for war on Iran but not for public housing. articles.title: Ecuador Pushes to Expand Amazon Oil Drilling While Land Defenders Face Threats
articles.content_excerpt: Ecuadorians voted overwhelmingly in 2023 to stop oil extraction at Yasuní National Park, one of the most biodiverse places on Earth, yet oil drilling has continued despite that historic referendum. “The government does not want to close the wells,” says Ivonne Yánez, the president of Acción Ecológica, an environmental nonprofit group based in Ecuador. The Ecuadorian government is also “continuing expanding the oil activities in the Amazon,” she points out. Yánez also speaks about how dangerous Latin America is for environmental activists. It is where “the most number of defenders that are just defending their lands, their rivers, their rights,” are killed. “And in Ecuador, this is also happening.”

articles.title: Ebola deaths in DRC cross 5,500 as armed attacks and funding shortages impede containment
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content_excerpt: The fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record has killed 5,568 people , nearly half of the 11,376 confirmed cases are in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) as of Saturday, November 14. “If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it will be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the continent’s highest health body, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), told Reuters on Sunday. The world’s worst on record so far is the West Africa outbreak, infecting 28,600 people and killing more than 11,000 over a period of two years from 2014 to 2016.
